synopsis: Test selection is a safety decision, not simply a way to shrink a giant matrix: the booklet recommends predefined coverage models, hazard-driven scenario classes, equivalence classes, boundary analysis and uncertainty sampling rather than an exhaustive Cartesian product [f14074, f5470, f11042, f13297]. No single method provides discrete-configuration coverage, continuous-parameter coverage, failure discovery and field-rate estimation; coverage designs, failure-seeking searches and a separate frozen statistical sample must serve different purposes [f6798, f14098]. Reported success across 20,000 scenarios is not statistically meaningful without a defined population and selection mechanism, and failure-hunting searches cannot report a failure rate [f6933, f14096]. Prioritization should use accident data, especially fatality patterns, while frequency and damage estimates are weaker evidence; safety-critical interactions still require hazard analysis, field failures and engineering knowledge [f10622, f11605, f4076]. Reported efficiencies include NIST test-set reductions of 20–700 times and on-road dense-reinforcement-learning acceleration of 10^3–10^5 times, but the latter is not proven off-road and requires a large naturalistic dataset for legitimate evaluation claims [f6820, f7078, f7079, f7277]. An initial statistical plan and coverage metrics are considered realistic by mid-2027 for a team starting in October 2026, but no universal off-road coverage prescription was found; within a four-month window, the recommended hybrid approach uses simulation for screening and informative physical-test selection rather than proof by itself [f846, f5475, f13496, f9697, f14059].
